questions.solution:
**B lymphocytes** differentiate into **plasma cells**, which secrete antibodies — this is **humoral** immunity.

**T lymphocytes** mediate **cell-mediated** immunity: they attack infected cells directly and help coordinate the response, but they do not secrete antibodies.

The distinction matters in transplantation, where graft rejection is T-cell mediated.

questions.q: An antibody molecule has the structure:
options: $\text{H}_2\text{L}_2$ — two heavy and two light chains
questions.solution:
An antibody is $\mathbf{\text{H}_2\text{L}_2}$ — two identical **heavy** chains and two identical **light** chains, held by disulphide bonds in a Y shape.

The tips of the Y are the **variable** regions, which differ between antibodies and give the specificity for a particular antigen. The stem is constant and determines the class — IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE, IgD.

Having two identical binding sites is what lets antibodies cross-link antigens and clump them together.

HIV targets **helper T cells** ($\text{CD}4^{+}$), which are the coordinators of the whole immune response — they activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells alike.

Destroying them cripples both humoral and cell-mediated immunity at once, which is why AIDS leaves the patient open to **opportunistic infections** that a healthy immune system dismisses easily.

HIV is a **retrovirus**: it carries RNA and uses **reverse transcriptase** to make DNA that integrates into the host genome, which is why the infection is lifelong.

A vaccine introduces a harmless form of the antigen, so the body makes **its own** antibodies and, crucially, **memory cells**. That makes it **active**; being deliberately induced makes it **artificial**.

The four types are worth keeping straight:

**Active natural** — recovering from an infection.

**Active artificial** — vaccination.

**Passive natural** — antibodies crossing the placenta or in breast milk.

**Passive artificial** — an injection of ready-made antibodies, as in antivenom.

Only the **active** kinds give lasting protection, because only they create memory cells. Passive immunity acts at once but fades.

Malaria is caused by the protozoan **Plasmodium**, transmitted by the bite of the **female Anopheles** mosquito, which is the vector rather than the cause.

The fever spikes every 48 or 72 hours because the parasite bursts out of red blood cells in synchronised waves, releasing the toxin **haemozoin**.

Only the female mosquito bites, since she needs a blood meal for her eggs.

questions.q: The property that distinguishes a malignant tumour from a benign one is:
options: Metastasis, the ability to spread to other tissues
questions.solution:
**Metastasis** — cells break away, travel in the blood or lymph, and start new tumours elsewhere — is the defining property of a **malignant** tumour.

A **benign** tumour stays confined to its original site and is usually removable.

Metastasis is what makes cancer lethal and difficult to treat: a localised mass can be excised, but cells already dispersed through the body cannot be.

questions.q: Morphine and heroin are obtained from:
questions.solution:
Morphine, and heroin (diacetylmorphine) made from it, come from the latex of **Papaver somniferum**, the opium poppy.

They are **depressants** and powerful **analgesics** — morphine is still a mainstay of surgical pain relief. They are also strongly addictive.

Cannabinoids come from **Cannabis sativa** and cocaine from the coca plant, which is a stimulant rather than a depressant.

questions.q: Which is an example of an **innate** immune barrier?
questions.solution:
Innate immunity is **non-specific** and present from birth. It has four kinds of barrier:

**Physical** — skin and mucus membranes

**Physiological** — stomach acid, saliva, tears

**Cellular** — macrophages, neutrophils, natural killer cells

**Cytokine** — interferons released by virus-infected cells

Antibodies, memory cells and lymphocytes belong to **acquired** immunity, which is specific and, crucially, has **memory**.

questions.q: An allergic reaction is mediated mainly by which antibody class?
questions.solution:
**IgE** binds to mast cells and basophils. When the allergen cross-links it, those cells release **histamine** and serotonin, producing the sneezing, watering eyes and inflammation.

Antihistamines work by blocking histamine receptors.

An allergy is therefore not a weak immune system but an **over-reaction** to something harmless — the machinery is working, just aimed at the wrong target.

questions.q: How many polypeptide chains are there in one antibody molecule?
questions.solution: Two heavy chains and two light chains: $2 + 2 = \mathbf{4}$ polypeptide chains, giving the $\text{H}_2\text{L}_2$ structure.

questions.q: How many antigen-binding sites does a single IgG antibody molecule have?
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{2}$ — one at each tip of the Y, formed where a heavy and a light chain's variable regions meet.

Having two identical sites is what lets an antibody **cross-link** two antigens and clump them into a precipitate, which is how agglutination works. IgM, a pentamer, has ten.

questions.q: Below approximately what $\text{CD}4^{+}$ cell count per microlitre is an HIV infection classified as AIDS?
questions.solution:
AIDS is diagnosed when the $\text{CD}4^{+}$ count falls below about $\mathbf{200}$ cells per microlitre, or when an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection appears.

A healthy count is roughly $500$ to $1500$ per microlitre.

questions.q: In malaria caused by Plasmodium vivax, the fever recurs approximately every how many hours?
questions.solution:
Every $\mathbf{48}$ hours, giving the pattern known as **tertian** fever.

The rhythm reflects the synchronised bursting of infected red blood cells, which releases the toxin haemozoin. **Plasmodium malariae** gives a 72-hour (quartan) cycle.

questions.q: How many main classes of immunoglobulin are found in humans?
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{5}$ classes: **IgG**, **IgM**, **IgA**, **IgE** and **IgD**.

IgG is the commonest and the only one crossing the placenta; IgM appears first in an infection; IgA guards mucosal surfaces and is in breast milk; IgE mediates allergy; IgD's role is a receptor on B cells.

questions.q: Distinguish between innate and acquired immunity. Explain the primary and secondary immune responses, and use the difference between them to explain how vaccination protects against disease.
questions.solution:
**Innate immunity** is present from birth, acts immediately, and is **non-specific** — the same response whatever the invader. It has four kinds of barrier:

**Physical** — the skin, and mucus lining the respiratory and digestive tracts

**Physiological** — stomach acid, saliva, tears

**Cellular** — macrophages, neutrophils and natural killer cells, which engulf or destroy invaders

**Cytokine** — interferons, released by virus-infected cells, which warn neighbouring cells

It has **no memory**: the thousandth encounter is met exactly like the first.

**Acquired immunity** develops after exposure, is **specific** to a particular antigen, and — the property that matters most — has **memory**.

It has two arms. **Humoral** immunity uses B lymphocytes, which become plasma cells and secrete **antibodies** into the blood, dealing with pathogens outside cells. **Cell-mediated** immunity uses T lymphocytes, which attack **infected cells** directly and reject grafts.

**The primary response.** On first exposure:

- There is a **lag of several days** while the few lymphocytes with a matching receptor are found and multiplied — clonal selection takes time.
- **IgM** appears first, in **low** concentration.
- The response is **slow and weak**, and the person usually falls ill.
- Crucially, some activated lymphocytes become **memory cells** and persist, sometimes for life.

**The secondary response.** On a later exposure to the same antigen:

- The lag is **very short**, hours rather than days, because a large population of memory cells is already present and already specific.
- **IgG** predominates, at a concentration perhaps a **hundred to a thousand times** higher.
- The response is **faster, larger and longer-lasting**, and the pathogen is usually destroyed before symptoms appear.

**How vaccination uses this.**

A vaccine is a preparation of the pathogen's antigens in a form that **cannot cause the disease** — killed or inactivated organisms, a weakened (attenuated) strain, a purified surface protein, a toxoid, or mRNA encoding a viral protein.

It triggers a **primary response**. The person makes antibodies and, far more importantly, **memory cells** — but without ever suffering the illness.

When the real pathogen later arrives, it meets a **secondary** response. The immune system is already primed, the response is immediate and overwhelming, and the infection is cleared before it can establish itself.

**So vaccination does not give immunity directly — it gives the immune system a rehearsal.** The protection comes entirely from the memory cells the vaccine leaves behind. That is exactly why a vaccine takes a week or two to become effective and is useless given during an outbreak already underway in that person.

**Why passive immunisation is different.** For a snake bite or a tetanus wound, there is no time for a primary response. **Ready-made antibodies** are injected instead. That works within minutes, but it creates **no memory cells**, so the protection lasts only until those borrowed antibodies are degraded — a few weeks. It is a treatment, not a vaccination.

**Herd immunity** follows from all this: once enough of a population carries memory cells, the pathogen cannot find enough susceptible hosts to spread, which protects even those who were never vaccinated. That is how smallpox was eradicated, and it is the reason vaccination coverage is measured as a population figure rather than an individual one.
